title: Evaluate basic external animal anatomy and morphology

lessons.title: Know the parts of the animal
lessons.html:
Why learn the body parts?

You work with animals every day. If you know the names of the body parts, you can tell your supervisor where an animal is hurt. This helps the animal get help fast.

Parts of a cow

  • Head: ears, eyes, nose (muzzle), mouth, horns.
  • Neck: under the neck is loose skin called the dewlap.
  • Chest: the front part between the front legs is the brisket.
  • Back: the top of the shoulders is the withers. Then the back, the hips and the rump.
  • Tail and tail head.
  • Belly and flank: the soft side behind the ribs is the flank.
  • Legs: knee in front, hock at the back, and the hoof with two claws.
  • Udder and teats on cows.

Other animals

  • Sheep: wool on the body, two claws on each foot.
  • Goat: hair, often a beard and horns.
  • Pig: flat nose called a snout, many teats.
  • Chicken: beak, comb on top of the head, wattles under the beak, feathers, two legs.
  • Horse: one solid hoof on each foot, mane on the neck.

Point to each part when you work with the animals and say its name. This is the best way to learn.

lessons.title: Is this animal healthy and well built?
lessons.html:
Look at the animal every day

Stand back and look at the animal from the side, front and back. Then watch it walk.

Signs of a healthy animal

  • Bright, clear eyes.
  • Clean, wet nose in cattle.
  • Shiny coat or good wool.
  • Walks well on all four legs.
  • Eats and drinks well. Cattle, sheep and goats chew the cud.
  • Stays with the group.

Signs of a problem

  • Limping or not wanting to walk.
  • Runny eyes or nose.
  • Swelling, wounds or lumps.
  • Very thin, with ribs and hip bones showing.
  • Standing alone, head down.
  • Hard, hot or swollen udder.

Tell your supervisor about any problem right away.

Fat or thin?

Put your hand on the back and ribs.

What you feelCondition
Sharp bones, no fatToo thin
Bones felt with a little pushGood
Cannot feel bones, lumps of fatToo fat

Well built

A good animal has straight strong legs, a straight back, a good mouth and a good udder or testes. These animals live longer and give more meat, milk or wool.

An animal with bad legs cannot walk far in the veld to find grass and water. An animal with a bad mouth cannot eat well. A cow with a bad udder cannot feed her calf. Your supervisor may choose not to keep these animals for breeding, so tell them when you see such faults.

lessons.title: Looking at teeth and handling safely
lessons.html:
Teeth show age

Cattle, sheep and goats have teeth only at the bottom in the front. At the top there is a hard pad.

  • Young animals have small milk teeth.
  • As they grow, two big teeth come out first. This animal is a two-tooth.
  • Then four, then six, then eight big teeth. Eight is a full mouth.
  • Old animals lose teeth. This is a broken mouth. It cannot eat well.

Handle animals safely

  • Work slowly and quietly. Do not shout or hit.
  • Put cattle in a crush before you look at them closely.
  • Never stand right behind a cow or horse. It can kick.
  • Hold a sheep under the jaw and by the side. Do not pull its wool.
  • Open the mouth from the side. Keep fingers away from the back teeth.
  • Wash your hands after work.

Tell and write

When you find a problem, tell your supervisor:

  1. The animal's number or tag.
  2. What you saw.
  3. Where on the body, using the right name.

For example: Cow 214 is limping on the left back leg, there is a swelling above the hoof.

Key points

  • Learn the names of body parts such as brisket, withers, flank and hock.
  • A healthy animal has bright eyes, eats well and walks well.
  • Feel the back and ribs to see if an animal is too thin or too fat.
  • Teeth show age, from milk teeth to full mouth.
  • Never stand behind a cow or horse, and report problems at once.
